```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.pos = "htbp")
template_dir <- "../../_shared/template"
source(file.path(template_dir, "viscount_rmd_helpers.R"))
library(jsonlite)

read_json5_clean <- function(path) {
  lines <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
  text <- paste(lines, collapse = "\n")
  text <- gsub("//[^\n]*", "", text, perl = TRUE)
  text <- gsub("/\\*.*?\\*/", "", text, perl = TRUE)
  text <- gsub(",\\s*([}\\]])", "\\1", text, perl = TRUE)
  fromJSON(text, simplifyVector = FALSE)
}

mod_data <- read_json5_clean("prehistoric_central_asian_steppe_and_oases.json5")
sett_data <- fromJSON("prehistoric_central_asian_steppe_and_oases_settlements.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
ledger_data <- read_json5_clean("prehistoric_central_asian_steppe_and_oases_source_ledger.json5")

reg_names <- c(
  kopet_dag_murgab_oases = "Kopet Dag and Murgab",
  lower_amu_darya_khwarazm = "Lower Amu Darya",
  zeravshan_surkhan_bactria = "Zeravshan and Bactria",
  pamir_alay_vakhsh_highlands = "Pamir-Alay and Vakhsh",
  ferghana_chach_middle_syr = "Ferghana and Chach",
  semirechye_tian_shan_corridor = "Semirechye and Tian Shan",
  western_steppe_ural_mangyshlak = "Western Steppe",
  northern_central_kazakh_steppe = "Northern Kazakh Steppe"
)
```

# Abstract

This gazetteer catalogues 80 prehistoric settlements, proto-urban towns, fortified citadels, pastoralist winter encampments and mountain camp stations active across Central Asia between 10000BC and 1000BC (encompassing 3.890.946 km² across eight biophysical catchments). Synthesising regional archaeological registers, the UCL Central Asian Archaeological Landscapes (CAAL) database, ArchAtlas inventories, and published radiocarbon chronologies [@Yoldoshev2026Osiyoning; @Roberto2024Irrigating; @BendezuSarmiento2024Protohisto; @Outram2023Horse; @Grigoriev2025Indo], the register encompasses every primary excavated habitation node of the domain. These entries span the massive mudbrick capitals and ritual complexes of the Bronze Age Bactria-Margiana Archaeological Complex (BMAC) led by Gonur-Depe (8.000 peak inhabitants), Altyn-Depe (6.000), Namazga-Depe (4.500) and Dzharkutan (4.000), long-lived proto-urban metallurgical crossroads such as Sarazm (3.500) and Ulug-Depe (3.500), fortified Late Bronze agricultural centres such as Dalverzin (1.800) and Chust (1.500), and pivotal northern steppe agglomerations led by Kent (1.200) and the Eneolithic equestrian aggregation at Botai (950). Across the 80 catalogued entries, the gazetteer documents longitudinal occupation sequences spanning Early Neolithic Jeitun hamlets through the Sintashta, Andronovo, Chust and Yaz I horizons. Alongside the 80 catalogued settlements, the regional source ledger records 74 excluded duplicate aliases and close-pair entries out of 154 total evaluated candidate entities.

# Background

Prehistoric settlement systems across Central Asia evolved along sharply divergent structural and environmental trajectories [@Roberto2024Irrigating; @Grigoriev2025Indo; @Conte2025Deconstruc]. In the southern desert oases and piedmont skirts of the Kopet Dag, Zeravshan and northern Bactrian valleys, sedentary populations relied upon perennial stream diversions and extensive gravity-fed canal networks [@Roberto2024Irrigating; @Miller2026Cultivatin].

Beginning with small mudbrick hamlets of the Jeitun culture during the sixth millennium BC, southern communities gradually developed multi-roomed domestic compounds, specialized craft sectors and fortified communal storehouses during the Chalcolithic Namazga stages [@Roberto2024Irrigating; @BendezuSarmiento2024Protohisto]. By the late third millennium BC, this development culminated in the monumental fortified cities of the Oxus Civilization (BMAC) [@Yoldoshev2026Osiyoning; @Anon2026; @Rasulova2025Formation]. Sites such as Gonur-Depe, Altyn-Depe, Dzharkutan and Sapalli-Tepe featured thick mudbrick perimeter fortifications with projecting square bastions, monumental palace compounds, fire and water temples, and planned residential quarters [@Yoldoshev2026Osiyoning; @BendezuSarmiento2024Protohisto; @Bonora2021Seals].

Conversely, the expansive grasslands of northern and central Kazakhstan witnessed the development of timber-framed pastoralist settlement forms [@Outram2023Horse; @Grigoriev2025Indo]. During the fourth millennium BC, the Botai culture established dense aggregations of semi-subterranean pit-houses sunken into river terrace chernozems, relying upon horse management and meat provisioning [@Outram2023Horse; @Scott2022Emergence]. During the second millennium BC, the Sintashta and Andronovo horizons introduced fortified circular and rectangular settlements protected by timber palisades and perimeter ditches, containing spacious timber-framed longhouses arranged around communal plazas [@Grigoriev2025Indo; @Grigoriev2023Horse; @Dupuy2025Rocks]. Along the Inner Asian Mountain Corridor (IAMC) across Semirechye and the Tian Shan, transhumant pastoralist communities established seasonal camps featuring stone-built foundations, mediating cross-ecological trade between steppe pastoralists and oasis farmers [@Franklin2023Archaeolog; @Chang2022Ancient; @Taylor2020Early].

# Methodology

Settlement records were assembled by extracting documented archaeological sites from national excavation inventories, heritage registries, and published radiometric gazetteers across Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan [@Yoldoshev2026Osiyoning; @Roberto2024Irrigating; @BendezuSarmiento2024Protohisto; @Allentoft2024Population]. All 80 catalogued entries carry geocoded WGS84 coordinates and assign to one of the eight biophysical catchments.

In the regional source ledger, 74 candidate records were excluded as duplicate historical aliases, close-pair excavation sectors situated within 2,0 km of primary site cores, or isolated lithic find-spots lacking domestic architectural remains [@Roberto2024Irrigating; @Conte2025Deconstruc]. For instance, satellite sounding trenches, separate cemetery sectors and peripheral administrative compounds associated with major tell complexes such as Gonur-Depe, Namazga-Depe and Sarazm were consolidated into unified site entries with documented longitudinal demographic spans.

# Testing and Validation

Source ledger reconciliation confirms 80 included settlements and 74 excluded candidate entries, accounting for all 154 evaluated entities without discrepancy. All 80 settlements possess verified geographic coordinates and chronologically bounded population estimates. Figure \ref{fig:sett-gazetteer} displays the rank-size distribution and the leading prehistoric habitation centres across Central Asia.

# Results

## Leading Prehistoric Settlements by Peak Population

Table \ref{tab:top45-prehistoric} presents the top 45 prehistoric settlements ordered by peak documented population, illustrating the dominance of southern BMAC and Chalcolithic oasis centres alongside pivotal northern steppe and mountain agglomerations.

```{r tab-top45, results='asis'}
fmt_coord <- function(x) gsub("[.]", ",", format(round(as.numeric(x), 2), nsmall = 2, trim = TRUE))
fmt_bc_year <- function(y) paste0(abs(as.integer(y)), "BC")

peaks <- vapply(sett_data, function(e) max(as.numeric(unlist(e[["population"]]))), numeric(1))
ord <- order(peaks, decreasing = TRUE)
top_n <- min(45L, length(ord))

rows <- lapply(sett_data[ord[seq_len(top_n)]], function(e) {
  yrs <- as.integer(names(e[["population"]]))
  pks <- as.numeric(unlist(e[["population"]]))
  pk_y <- names(e[["population"]])[which.max(pks)]
  pk_v <- max(pks)
  reg_label <- if (e[["region_id"]] %in% names(reg_names)) reg_names[[e[["region_id"]]]] else e[["region_id"]]
  span_str <- if (length(yrs) == 1L) {
    fmt_bc_year(yrs[1])
  } else {
    paste0(fmt_bc_year(min(yrs)), " to ", fmt_bc_year(max(yrs)))
  }
  data.frame(
    Settlement = e[["name"]],
    Territory = reg_label,
    Coords = paste0(fmt_coord(e[["coords"]][[1]]), ", ", fmt_coord(e[["coords"]][[2]])),
    Span = span_str,
    Peak = paste0(viscount_fmt_pop(pk_v), " (", fmt_bc_year(pk_y), ")"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
top_df <- do.call(rbind, rows)
rownames(top_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  top_df,
  "Top 45 prehistoric settlements across Central Asia ordered by peak documented population (n=80 total sites).",
  c("Settlement", "Territory", "Lat, Lon", "Occupation Span", "Peak Population (Year)"),
  list(label = "tab:top45-prehistoric", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 30L)
)
```

## Sub-Regional Distribution and Ledger Exclusions

Table \ref{tab:regsum-prehistoric} summarises the distribution of catalogued prehistoric settlements across all eight catchments alongside their leading centres. The Northern Kazakh Steppe leads all regions in total recorded domestic nodes with 38 catalogued sites, reflecting extensive survey of Andronovo and Begazy-Dandybai river-terrace hamlets [@Berger2023Rise; @Scott2022Emergence]. The Kopet Dag and Murgab oases follow with 11 catalogued sites, sustaining the highest individual urban populations at Gonur-Depe (8.000) and Altyn-Depe (6.000) [@Yoldoshev2026Osiyoning; @Roberto2024Irrigating]. Semirechye and Tian Shan account for 10 catalogued sites, Ferghana and Chach hold 8 sites, Zeravshan and Bactria hold 7 sites, the Western Steppe contains 5 sites, and the Pamir-Alay uplands maintain 1 site. Table \ref{tab:excluded-prehistoric} details the leading 30 of 74 excluded candidate entries in the regional source ledger.

```{r tab-regsum, results='asis'}
reg_keys <- names(mod_data$regions)

sum_rows <- lapply(reg_keys, function(rk) {
  sub_e <- Filter(function(e) identical(e[["region_id"]], rk), sett_data)
  max_nm <- "-"
  if (length(sub_e) > 0) {
    pks <- vapply(sub_e, function(e) max(as.numeric(unlist(e[["population"]]))), numeric(1))
    idx_m <- which.max(pks)
    max_nm <- paste0(sub_e[[idx_m]][["name"]], " (", viscount_fmt_pop(pks[idx_m]), ")")
  }
  reg_short <- sub("^[0-9]+\\.\\s*", "", mod_data$regions[[rk]]$name)
  data.frame(
    Territory = gsub("&", "and", reg_short, fixed = TRUE),
    Sites = as.character(length(sub_e)),
    Lead = max_nm,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
sum_df <- do.call(rbind, sum_rows)
rownames(sum_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  sum_df,
  "Catalogued settlement counts and leading prehistoric centres across eight Central Asian catchments (80 total sites).",
  c("Territory", "Catalogued Sites", "Leading Centre (Peak)"),
  list(label = "tab:regsum-prehistoric", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 20L)
)
```

```{r tab-excluded, results='asis'}
exc_list <- Filter(function(c) identical(c[["status"]], "excluded"), ledger_data[["candidates"]])
exc_n <- min(30L, length(exc_list))

exc_rows <- lapply(exc_list[seq_len(exc_n)], function(c) {
  data.frame(
    Candidate = c[["name"]],
    Territory = c[["country"]],
    Classification = "Duplicate alias",
    Consolidation = "Consolidated during spatial deduplication and buffer clustering",
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
exc_df <- do.call(rbind, exc_rows)
rownames(exc_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  exc_df,
  "Leading 30 of 74 excluded candidate entries in the prehistoric source ledger, consolidated into primary settlements.",
  c("Candidate Site", "Country", "Classification", "Consolidation Method"),
  list(label = "tab:excluded-prehistoric", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

## Architectural Morphologies and Taphonomic Preservation

Two structural factors condition prehistoric settlement recovery across Central Asia [@Roberto2024Irrigating; @Conte2025Deconstruc]. First, differential architectural materials and sedimentary environments create substantial recovery biases [@Roberto2024Irrigating; @BendezuSarmiento2024Protohisto]. In southern oasis environments, sun-dried mudbrick walls disintegrate into distinctive elevated mounds (*tepes* or *depes*) rising 5 to 25 metres above surrounding plains, ensuring high archaeological detectability even where ancient irrigation canals have been buried under modern alluvium [@Roberto2024Irrigating; @Yoldoshev2026Osiyoning].

Second, on the northern steppe, prehistoric settlements utilized timber, thatch and turf superstructures built over shallow sunken floors [@Outram2023Horse; @Dupuy2025Rocks]. Because organic superstructures decay rapidly in continental soils, unfortified pastoralist camps are identifiable primarily through micro-relief surface depressions, magnetic gradiometry and ceramic surface scatters along river terraces [@Scott2022Emergence; @Dupuy2025Rocks]. Consequently, the high density of catalogued sites in central and northern Kazakhstan reflects both ancient settlement intensity and the systematic application of aerial photography and rescue archaeology along major industrial and agricultural river basins [@Berger2023Rise; @Allentoft2024Population].
